lessons.title: Understand Ratios
lessons.objective: I can write and describe a ratio that compares two quantities.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain a comparison using the words ratio, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and colon notation.

concept.heading: What is a ratio?
concept.intro: A ratio compares two amounts. It tells how much of one thing there is for another thing.
concept.keyIdea: Understanding Ratios. Formula: a : b | a to b | a/b. 1. A ratio compares two quantities; order of quantities matters. 2. Part-to-Part compares two distinct subgroups (e.g. boys to girls). 3. Part-to-Whole compares one subgroup to the total (e.g. boys to class)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Chef Reyes uses 3 cups of apple juice for every 2 cups of sparkling water.
I am comparing two amounts: apple juice and sparkling water.
I write apple juice to sparkling water, in that order, as 3 to 2, or 3:2.
I can also draw the ratio. On a tape diagram I give apple juice 3 equal parts and sparkling water 2 equal parts, so one batch is 5 parts in all.
Those same 5 parts show a second ratio: apple juice to the whole fruit drink is 3 to 5.
On a double number line I line the two amounts up: 5 cups of fruit drink pairs with 3 cups of apple juice, and 10 cups of fruit drink pairs with 6 cups of apple juice.
linesEs: El chef Reyes usa 3 tazas de jugo de manzana por cada 2 tazas de agua mineral.
Estoy comparando dos cantidades: jugo de manzana y agua mineral.
Escribo jugo de manzana a agua mineral, en ese orden, como 3 a 2, o 3:2.
También puedo dibujar la razón. En un diagrama de barras le doy al jugo de manzana 3 partes iguales y al agua mineral 2 partes iguales, así que una tanda son 5 partes en total.
Esas mismas 5 partes muestran una segunda razón: jugo de manzana al total de la bebida es 3 a 5.
En una recta numérica doble alineo las dos cantidades: 5 tazas de bebida se emparejan con 3 tazas de jugo de manzana, y 10 tazas de bebida se emparejan con 6 tazas de jugo de manzana.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: A bowl has 4 apples and 1 orange. What two amounts are we comparing?
We write apples to oranges in order: 4 to 1, or 4:1.
Now draw it: 4 equal parts for apples beside 1 part for oranges, 5 parts of fruit in all.
So apples to total fruit is 4 to 5.
linesEs: Un tazón tiene 4 manzanas y 1 naranja. ¿Qué dos cantidades estamos comparando?
Escribimos manzanas a naranjas en orden: 4 a 1, o 4:1.
Ahora dibújalo: 4 partes iguales para las manzanas junto a 1 parte para la naranja, 5 partes de fruta en total.
Entonces manzanas al total de fruta es 4 a 5.

vocabulary.example: 3 red tiles to 5 blue tiles can be written 3:5 or 3/5.

A ratio comparing one part to the whole group.

lessons.title: Understand Rates and Unit Rates
lessons.objective: I can describe a rate using its two different units and use a model to find a travel time, and I can find a unit rate to compare prices and decide the better buy.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain a rate like "150 miles per hour" using distance and time units, and explain my choice using the words rate, unit rate, per, and better buy.

concept.heading: What is a unit rate, and how does it help me find the better buy?
concept.intro: A rate compares two amounts with different units. A unit rate tells you the amount for just 1 of something, like the cost for 1 game.
concept.keyIdea: Rates & Unit Rates. Formula: Unit Rate = (Total Quantity) ÷ (Number of Units). 1. Rate: A ratio comparing two quantities with different units (e.g. $12 for 3 lbs). 2. Unit Rate: A rate simplified to a denominator of 1 unit ($4 per 1 lb). 3. Divide numerator by denominator to compute the per-one amount

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Booth A charges $3 for 5 games. I want the cost for just 1 game.
I divide the cost by the games: $3 ÷ 5 = $0.60.
So Booth A costs $0.60 per game. That is the unit rate.
Because this unit rate is money for one item, it has its own name: it is the unit price.
Now I can compare this booth's unit price fairly with any other booth's.
linesEs: El puesto A cobra $3 por 5 partidas. Quiero el costo de solo 1 partida.
Divido el costo entre las partidas: $3 ÷ 5 = $0.60.
Entonces el puesto A cuesta $0.60 por partida. Esa es la tasa unitaria.
Como esta tasa unitaria es dinero por un artículo, tiene su propio nombre: es el precio unitario.
Ahora puedo comparar de forma justa el precio unitario de este puesto con el de cualquier otro.

support.prompt: A recipe uses 4 cups of milk and 1 cup of cream. What is the ratio of milk to cream?
support.explanation: A ratio compares quantities in the order given. Milk to cream = 4 to 1, or 4:1.
feedback: The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
You added the numbers together — a ratio compares two amounts, not their sum.
5 is the total number of cups, not the amount of cream. This compares the whole recipe to one part instead of milk to cream.
hints: Re-read the question: it asks for milk to cream, in that exact order.
In a ratio, the amount named first goes first. Find the milk amount and the cream amount before you write anything.
Underline the two amounts: milk = 4 cups, cream = 1 cup. Write them in the same order the question names them.

support.prompt: Chef Reyes uses 6 strawberries and 2 bananas in a smoothie. What is the part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit?
support.explanation: Total fruit = 6 + 2 = 8. The part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit is 2:8.
feedback: This compares bananas to strawberries, which is part-to-part. A part-to-whole ratio needs the total number of pieces of fruit as the second number.
Re-check: does this show a part being compared to the whole group?
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
hints: Notice the word 'total' — this is a part-to-WHOLE ratio, not banana-to-strawberry.
First find the total fruit by adding strawberries and bananas. Then compare bananas to that total.
Add 6 + 2 to get the total fruit. Then write the bananas' number first, followed by that total.

support.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 are girls. What is the part-to-part ratio of boys to girls?
support.explanation: Boys = 30 − 18 = 12. Part-to-part ratio of boys to girls = 12:18. (Order matters!)
feedback: You found the number of boys correctly, but 30 is the whole class. That makes this part-to-whole, and the question asks boys compared to girls.
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
You added the numbers together — a ratio compares two amounts, not their sum.
hints: The problem tells you girls (18) and the whole class (30) — but it asks about BOYS to girls.
Find the number of boys first by subtracting the girls from the class total. Then write boys first, girls second.
Subtract 30 − 18 to find the boys. Put that number first in the ratio, then 18 for the girls.

support.prompt: A pet store has 5 dogs and 9 cats. What is the ratio of dogs to cats?
support.explanation: The ratio of dogs to cats compares dogs first, then cats: 5 to 9, or 5:9.
feedback: You added the numbers together — a ratio compares two amounts, not their sum.
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
14 is the total number of pets, and here it is written first. Check both the order of the words and whether the question asks about a total at all.
hints: Re-read: the question asks for dogs to cats, in that order.
A ratio only uses the two amounts being compared — don't add them together. Match the order to the words.
Dogs are named first, so their count (5) starts the ratio. Then write the cats' count after the colon.

support.prompt: Spot the Mistake — Order of a Ratio
steps: Read the problem: A salad bar has 5 bowls of soup and 8 sandwiches. Write the ratio of soup to sandwiches.
Identify the amounts: Soup = 5 and sandwiches = 8.
Write the ratio: A student writes the ratio of soup to sandwiches as 8:5.
Answer: The ratio of soup to sandwiches is 8:5.
support.explanation: The order matters. The problem asks for soup to sandwiches, so soup (5) must come first: the correct ratio is 5:8, not 8:5.
hints: Look at Step 3. Which amount should be written first — soup or sandwiches?
Soup is named first, so the ratio is 5:8. The student reversed the order.

support.prompt: A booth charges $4.50 for 9 games. What is the unit rate?
feedback: Double-check your division: $4.50 ÷ 9 — is it $0.45 or $0.50?
Divide the cost by the number of games: $4.50 ÷ 9, not some other operation.
That's the total cost for all 9 games, not the cost for one game.
hints: You know the total cost ($4.50) and the total games (9). A unit rate tells the cost of just ONE game.
To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of games so the second quantity becomes 1.
Set up the division: $4.50 ÷ 9. Think of $4.50 as 450 cents if that makes the division easier.

support.prompt: A car travels 180 miles using 6 gallons of gas. What is the unit rate in miles per gallon?
feedback: That's the number of gallons — you need to divide 180 by 6, not use 6 as the answer.
Check your division: 180 ÷ 6 — is it 30 or 36?
That's the total miles — divide 180 by 6 to find miles for one gallon.
hints: Notice the units in the question: miles PER gallon. That tells you miles go on top and gallons on the bottom.
Divide the total miles by the total gallons so you get the miles for just 1 gallon.
Start the division: 180 ÷ 6. Think: 6 × what number lands on 180?

support.prompt: A pack of 8 markers costs $6.00. What is the cost per marker?
feedback: This is what you get from splitting $6.00 into 10 parts, not 8. The number of markers in the pack is what you divide by.
That looks like an estimate rather than the exact quotient. Divide $6.00 by 8 carefully and keep both decimal places.
You may have divided backwards: try $6.00 ÷ 8, not 8 ÷ 6.
hints: You have 8 markers costing $6.00 total. 'Cost per marker' means the price of ONE marker.
Divide the total price by the number of markers — cost goes first, markers second.
Set up $6.00 ÷ 8. Tip: $6.00 is 600 cents, so try 600 ÷ 8 cents.

support.explanation: A unit rate has 1 in the second quantity. '12 miles per 1 hour' is the only choice where the second quantity is 1.
feedback: This is a rate, but is it for ONE hour or for 2 hours?
This is a rate, but is it for ONE gallon or for 3 gallons?
This is a rate, but is it for ONE game or for 5 games?
hints: A unit rate always compares to exactly ONE of something — look at the second number in each choice.
Check each choice: is the second quantity (hours, gallons, games) equal to 1? Only one choice passes that test.
Start with '24 miles in 2 hours' — the second quantity is 2, not 1, so that one is not a unit rate. Test the rest the same way.

steps: Read the problem: A booth charges $6.00 for 4 games. Find the unit rate (cost per game).
Set up the division: $6.00 ÷ 4 = $1.50, but the student writes $1.05 per game.
State the unit rate: The student says each game costs $1.05.
support.explanation: $6.00 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per game. The student divided correctly but wrote the digits in the wrong place value ($1.05 instead of $1.50). The cost per game is $1.50.
hints: Check the place value: is the answer about one dollar and a half, or one dollar and five cents?
Estimate first: $6.00 split into 4 games is more than $1.00 each, so $1.50 makes sense and $1.05 is too small.

core.prompt: A fruit salad has 5 pieces of melon, 3 pieces of pineapple, and 2 grapes. What is the ratio of pineapple to melon?
core.explanation: The ratio of pineapple to melon compares pineapple (3) to melon (5), so the ratio is 3:5.
feedback: That compares pineapple to the total (5 + 3 + 2). The question compares pineapple to melon only.
You started with the pineapple, which fits the order — but 2 is the number of grapes. Re-read which two amounts the question compares.
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
hints: Three fruits are listed, but the question only compares pineapple and melon — the grapes are extra info.
Pick out just the two amounts you need, then write them in the order the question names: pineapple first.
Circle the pineapple count (3) and the melon count (5). Write them in the order 'pineapple to melon.'

core.prompt: A parking lot has 10 cars and 6 trucks. What is the part-to-whole ratio of trucks to total vehicles?
core.explanation: Total vehicles = 10 + 6 = 16. The ratio of trucks to total is 6:16.
feedback: This compares trucks to cars, which is a part-to-part ratio. For part-to-whole you need 10 + 6 as the second number.
Re-check: does this show a part being compared to the whole group?
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
hints: The word 'total' means this is part-to-whole — compare trucks to ALL vehicles, not to cars.
First find the total number of vehicles by adding cars and trucks. The trucks' number goes first.
Add 10 + 6 to find the total vehicles. Then write 6 (the trucks) first and that total second.

steps: Read the problem: A class has 9 boys and 6 girls. Write the part-to-whole ratio of girls to the whole class.
Count the whole: 9 + 6 = 15 students in all.
Write the ratio: A student writes girls to the whole class as 6:9.
Answer: The part-to-whole ratio of girls to the whole class is 6:9.
core.explanation: Part-to-whole compares the part to the WHOLE (15), not to the other part. There are 6 girls and 15 students total, so the correct ratio is 6:15.
hints: Look at Step 3. A part-to-whole ratio should use the total from Step 2.
The student used 9 (just the boys) instead of the whole. The whole is 15, so girls to the whole class is 6:15.

core.prompt: Token packs: Pack A is 20 tokens for $5.00, Pack B is 35 tokens for $7.00, and Pack C is 50 tokens for $12.50. Which pack is the best deal per token?
core.explanation: Pack B has a unit rate of $0.20 per token, which is the lowest cost per token.
feedback: Compare the cost per token, not the total price or the total number of tokens. Divide each pack's price by its tokens and compare those results.
A bigger pack is not automatically cheaper for each token. Work out price ÷ tokens for every pack before deciding.
Compare the unit rates: $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25. Are all three the same?
hints: The 'best deal' is the pack where ONE token costs the least — not the pack with the most tokens.
Line up the three unit rates you found in the table and look for the smallest cost per token.
Compare $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25 per token. Which of those is the smallest amount of money?

core.prompt: Runner A completes 4 laps in 12 minutes. Runner B completes 5 laps in 14 minutes. Who runs more laps per minute?
core.explanation: Runner A: 4÷12 ≈ 0.33 laps/min. Runner B: 5÷14 ≈ 0.36 laps/min. Runner B runs slightly more laps per minute.
feedback: You found 4 ÷ 12, but compare: is 0.33 laps per minute more or less than 0.36?
Divide each runner's laps by their minutes. You should get two different rates.
You have the laps and the minutes for both runners — that's enough to find and compare their rates.
hints: Each runner has laps and minutes. 'More laps per minute' means you need each runner's laps-per-minute rate first.
Divide laps by minutes for BOTH runners, then compare the two decimals — bigger decimal means faster.
Start with Runner A: 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 laps per minute. Now find Runner B's rate with 5 ÷ 14 and compare.

steps: Read the problem: Pack X is 10 tokens for $4.00. Pack Y is 16 tokens for $6.00. Which is the better buy (lower cost per token)?
Compare the deals: Pack X costs $4.00 and Pack Y costs $6.00. The student says Pack X is the better buy because $4.00 is the lower total price.
State the answer: The student chooses Pack X.
core.explanation: Compare unit rates, not total prices. Pack X: $4.00 ÷ 10 = $0.40 per token. Pack Y: $6.00 ÷ 16 = $0.375 per token. Pack Y has the lower cost per token, so Pack Y is the better buy.
hints: A lower total price does not always mean a better buy — the packs have different numbers of tokens.
Find the cost per token for each pack by dividing cost by tokens, then compare those unit rates.

stretch.prompt: A bag of marbles has 8 red, 6 blue, and 4 green marbles. Write three different ratios using these quantities: one part-to-part ratio, one part-to-whole ratio, and explain the difference.
stretch.explanation: Part-to-part: red to blue = 8:6. Part-to-whole: green to total = 4:18. The difference is that part-to-part compares two individual groups, while part-to-whole compares one group to the entire collection (8 + 6 + 4 = 18).
hints: You need THREE things: a part-to-part ratio, a part-to-whole ratio, and an explanation of how they differ.
Part-to-part compares two colors. Part-to-whole compares one color to ALL marbles — so you'll need the total first.
Start by finding the whole: add 8 + 6 + 4. Then pick any two colors for your part-to-part ratio, like red to blue.

steps: Find the unit rate: 12 tickets for $8: 12 tickets for $8

To find 'dollars per ticket,' divide dollars by tickets: $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 per ticket.

stretch.prompt: An arcade sells tokens in three packs: 25 tokens for $5, 60 tokens for $10.80, and 100 tokens for $19. A student says the 100-token pack is always the best deal because you get the most tokens. Is the student correct? Find all three unit rates and explain.

The 60-token pack has the lowest unit rate, so it is the best deal — getting the most tokens is not the same as paying the least for each one.
hints: The student only looked at token COUNT. The question asks you to judge the deals by unit rate — cost per token.
Find dollars per token for all three packs by dividing each price by its tokens, then compare the three rates.
First pack: $5 ÷ 25 tokens = $0.20 per token. Now do $10.80 ÷ 60 and $19 ÷ 100, then see which rate is lowest.
